videoIdeas.title: The Prophetic Speaking Method Nobody Teaches You
videoIdeas.hook: You don't need a TED talk. You need to say it slow, clear, three times.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' post (1,899 views, strong save-worthy premise) proved this angle lands and it's one of your only pure public-speaking posts. doctordaanish and birdtart01 are both winning with practical 'save this' how-tos. This is a gap you own — nobody else in the niche is pulling public speaking from the Seerah.
videoIdeas.script:
You don't need a TED talk. You need to say it slow, clear, three times.

Anas ibn Malik narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ spoke, he'd repeat a sentence three times so it was understood. Not because people were slow. Because clarity is a responsibility, not a performance.

Most of you lose the room because you're rushing to sound smart. You cram five points into thirty seconds and nobody remembers one.

Pick the single line you want them to walk away with. Say it slow. Say it clear. Say it again.

1,400 years before anyone wrote a book on public speaking, the method was already there. We just stopped using it.

What's the one line you want people to leave your next talk with? Tell me below.

visuals.setting: Plain wall or bookshelf, mid-shot, you talking straight to camera, calm controlled energy — not hyped. Dark neutral clothing. Let the stillness do the work since the topic is slowness.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text appears one word at a time, slowly: 'SLOW.' then 'CLEAR.' then 'THREE TIMES.' — matching the cadence while you say the line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence as if you're correcting someone off-camera: 'No — say it again. Slower.'
Silent two-second pause on your face before the first word, with text 'Watch how he spoke' on screen
Split the screen: a fast rambling clip vs you saying one clear line, labelled

videoIdeas.title: Character Before Influence (Al-Qawi wal-Ameen)
videoIdeas.hook: Everyone wants to be followed. Almost nobody wants to be trustworthy first.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your '11 Prophetic Qualities of Leadership' post had the lowest engagement of the batch (1 comment) but the strongest evergreen premise — it was buried under a flat caption. The leadership pillar is barely represented in your top posts despite being a core pillar. Repackaging it with a sharper hook fills that gap.
videoIdeas.script:
Everyone wants to be followed. Almost nobody wants to be trustworthy first.

We chase influence before character. The Prophetic model reverses that completely.

The standard for leadership in the Qur'an is Al-Qawi wal-Ameen — strong and trustworthy. Competent and honest. In that order, both required.

Strength without trust is just a bully with a platform. Trust without competence is a nice guy who gets nothing done.

You want people to follow you? Stop asking how to get attention. Start asking whether you'd trust yourself with the thing you're asking them to give you.

Integrity comes first. It always did.

visuals.setting: Walking shot outdoors or in a corridor — movement matches the 'in that order' logic. Or seated, leaning forward, serious. Smart-casual, looks like someone who holds responsibility.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'Strong AND trustworthy' with the word 'AND' pulsing/enlarging to stress both are non-negotiable.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: start by pointing at camera — 'This is why nobody follows you'
Cold open with the Arabic 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen' on screen, no context, let curiosity pull them in
On-screen punchline held on the last frame: 'Integrity comes first' for the save

videoIdeas.title: There Is No 'Secular Job'
videoIdeas.hook: Ibn Sina, al-Biruni and Ibn al-Nafis wouldn't understand the phrase 'secular job'.
videoIdeas.rationale: This exact premise already pulled 1,707 views with zero caption effort and zero comments — meaning the idea carried it alone. Mindset is your most scalable pillar and doctordaanish's journaling/self-improvement angle shows the appetite. Reworking this as a full script with a call to engage should outperform the original.
videoIdeas.script:
Ibn Sina, al-Biruni, Ibn al-Nafis — three of the greatest minds in human history. Not one of them would understand the phrase 'secular job'.

To them, studying medicine, mapping the stars, understanding the body — that was worship. Knowledge and deen weren't two drawers. They were the same pursuit.

We built the wall between career and faith much later. And most of you didn't even build it. You inherited it. You just accepted that work is the dunya part and deen is the weekend part.

That split is making you miserable and it isn't even yours.

Your work can be an act of worship. But only if you stop treating it like a 9-to-5 interruption to your real life. It is your real life.

visuals.setting: Seated, warmer tone, slightly reflective energy — this is the 'sit down, let me tell you something' one. Books or a desk in frame to echo the scholars reference.
visuals.visualHook: Three names typed onto screen rapidly — 'Ibn Sina. Al-Biruni. Ibn al-Nafis.' — then a hard cut to your face for the hook line.
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text question overlay: 'Why do you think your job isn't ibadah?'
Cold open: 'The wall in your head isn't even yours' before explaining
Visual metaphor cut — a literal wall / two folders labelled 'deen' and 'career' being merged

videoIdeas.title: How To Actually Speak So People Remember You
videoIdeas.hook: Stop trying to be impressive. Start being clear. There's a difference and the room can tell.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart01's networking-questions video hit 2.1M views by giving practical, saveable scripts. You can own the Islamic/leadership version of 'here's exactly what to do.' You have almost no tactical public-speaking content despite it being a named pillar — pure gap.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop trying to be impressive. Start being clear. The room can tell the difference.

Three things that fix 90% of bad speaking, save this.

One. Cut your intro. Nobody needs 'so basically, um, I just wanted to kind of talk about.' Start with the point.

Two. One idea per breath. If you can't say it in a single clean sentence, you don't understand it well enough yet.

Three. Pause instead of filling. Silence feels long to you and powerful to them. The 'um' is you being scared of two seconds of quiet.

None of this is charisma. It's discipline. And discipline you can actually train.

Which one are you worst at? Be honest below.

visuals.setting: Clean, slightly brighter, direct-to-camera with high clarity energy — you're teaching. Number overlays as you count. Smart shirt.
visuals.visualHook: Big on-screen text '3 things. Save this.' snaps up on frame one with a subtle count sound.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: do the bad version first ('so, um, basically...') then cut sharply to 'Stop.'
Numbered text cards (1/2/3) that stamp on screen as each point lands
Hold the final frame on 'It's discipline, not charisma' for the save/share

videoIdeas.title: If You're In Your 20s As A Muslim, Read This
videoIdeas.hook: You're in your 20s and you think you have time. You have time. You don't have focus.
videoIdeas.rationale: doctordaanish's 'if you're in your 20s pls save this' hit 90K views and is running as a series. This save-bait listicle format is proven in your exact niche right now and you have no series. Doing your blunt, deen-rooted version is the single biggest format opportunity in this dataset.
videoIdeas.script:
You're in your 20s and you think you have time. You have time. What you don't have is focus.

Four things, before this decade spends you instead.

Stop collecting advice. You've watched 400 videos like this. You've applied none of them. Reps, not reels.

Pick your five people. The company you keep in your 20s is the man you become in your 30s. Audit them honestly.

Build something that outlives the dopamine. A skill, a habit, a halaqah, a business — anything you can't scroll past.

And fix your relationship with Allah now, while it's hard and quiet, not later when you're desperate.

Your 20s aren't a warm-up. This is the game. Save this and act on one of them today.

visuals.setting: Confident, grounded, mid-shot, slightly serious older-brother energy. Could film walking to signal momentum. Neutral strong outfit.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'Your 20s are not a warm-up.' holds for a beat before you speak.
otherHookIdeas: Number counter in corner (1/4, 2/4...) to signal a saveable list
Cold open with the blunt line pointed straight at the viewer, no smile
End-card punchline 'This is the game' frozen for shares, hinting 'part 2 coming' to build a series like doctordaanish

videoIdeas.title: Young Muslims Are Building Third Spaces And It Scares People
videoIdeas.hook: Young British Muslims are quietly building something, and the reaction tells you everything.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'third spaces' post (1,856 views) tapped community leadership — a real-world leadership angle that's distinct from the political content and more durable. It ties identity + leadership, which is underserved. Framing it as a movement gives it shareability without being a hot-take you'll regret.
videoIdeas.script:
Young British Muslims are quietly building something. Cafés. Community hubs. Study circles. Social events. Spaces where people can actually meet, build friendships, learn, and just belong.

And instead of celebrating it, some people see a threat.

Understand what's actually happening here. This is leadership without a title. No one appointed these people. They saw their community had nowhere to gather and they built it anyway.

That's the whole model. You don't wait to be given authority. You see a gap, you take responsibility for it, and you build.

The Ummah was never rebuilt by people waiting for permission. Stop waiting for someone to organise it. You're someone.

visuals.setting: Film in or near an actual community space / café / hall if possible — real environment adds weight. Warmer, slightly inspired-but-not-corny energy.
visuals.visualHook: B-roll quick cuts of a café, books, people gathering, then cut to your face for 'and the reaction tells you everything.'
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text: 'Leadership without a title' as the reframe lands
Cold open on the threat angle: 'Why does people gathering scare you?'
End on a direct-address freeze: 'You're someone.' for shares

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 8,579 views with 208 likes — your highest like count by far and a 2.4% like-to-view rate that beats most of your other posts. The hook ('Can't believe we're still discussing the necessity of protests in 2026') is a dated, incredulous opener that creates instant tension and a clear stance. This is proof your audience rewards a sharp, present-tense, 'I can't believe this' framing.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 12 comments against 208 likes — people agreed but didn't argue or add. The caption trails off mid-sentence ('make themselves feel bett'). Finish the thought and end on a direct question that forces a side ('Name one thing you've actually done this month') to convert those likes into comment-driven reach.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your highest-reach post at 8,613 views with 24 comments — the historical parallel (Iraq/Afghanistan → Iran, 'same guise') is a tight, memorable rhetorical structure. The repetition of 'under the guise' is exactly the kind of clean construction that travels. People shared this because the argument was pre-packaged for them.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 75 likes on 8.6K views is a low like rate for that reach — it spread but didn't resonate as 'mine.' There's no call to action and no tie to your pillars. Add a closing line that gives people something to carry or do, otherwise the reach is borrowed from the topic, not building loyalty to you.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your strongest on-brand post — the 'Slow. Clear. Three times.' public speaking angle from the Seerah is exactly your niche and the caption actually ends with a question ('What's the one line you want people to leave your next talk with?'). Clean hook, clear takeaway, pillar-aligned.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 3 comments despite a good question — the question came after a long caption most people won't read to the end. Put the question in the first line of the caption and as on-screen text in the video, and consider a 'save this' prompt since this is reference material people would store.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1,568 views on a pure leadership post ('Al-Qawi wal-Ameen, competent and trustworthy. Integrity comes first.') — the idea is excellent and the 'influence before character / the Prophetic model reverses that' framing is a genuinely strong reframe that deserves to be a flagship.

The caption reads like lecture notes ('📖 11 Prophetic Qualities of Leadership') which signals 'homework' not 'hook.' Lead with the blunt line ('Everyone wants to be followed, nobody wants to be trustworthy first') and cut the textbook framing.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1,707 views and a sharp, complete idea ('Ibn Sina... would not understand the phrase secular job. We built the wall between deen and career much later. Most of us just inherited it.') The short, punchy caption with line breaks is far more readable than your longer ones and the concept is highly shareable.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments on a genuinely provocative idea is a missed opportunity — you stated a position but didn't invite one. End with a direct prompt ('What job do you secretly think isn't ibadah?') and reuse this exact premise as the video script above; the concept is strong enough to be relaunched as a fuller piece.
